articles.title: Rhenus to double logistics space with new hub in Padua
articles.summary: Rhenus is expanding its logistics operations in Italy with a new 10,000 sqm hub at Interporto Padova. The facility will bring together transport, warehousing and freight forwarding services in one location. The company plans to begin moving operations to the new site in the first quarter of 2027. articles.body: Rhenus is expanding its logistics operations in Italy with a new 10,000 sqm hub at Interporto Padova. The facility will bring together transport, warehousing and freight forwarding services in one location. The company plans to begin moving operations to the new site in the first quarter of 2027. The move will double its covered logistics space in the Padua area from approximately 5,000 sqm to 10,000 sqm. The new hub will combine activities currently handled at two nearby warehouses. It will also increase Rhenus’ capacity to manage domestic and international freight. Bringing logistics services under one roof The facility will support road transport, air and ocean freight forwarding, warehousing and specialised delivery services. It will include 3,500 sqm for road transport operations and 3,000 sqm for Transport Related Warehousing, with space for approximately 3,000 pallets. Another 2,000 sqm will be dedicated to Special Delivery services, while 500 sqm will support the handling of dangerous goods under ADR requirements. The site will also feature more than 30 loading bays, office space and charging facilities for electric forklifts. Rhenus will transfer operations from its existing warehouses in Corso Spagna and Via Settima Strada. The move will take place gradually to maintain service continuity. Strengthening connections across Europe Interporto Padova provides access to major European transport routes, including the Mediterranean and Baltic-Adriatic corridors. The logistics centre also benefits from road and rail connections, with access to the A4 and A13 motorways and links to Venice and Verona airports. “With this hub, we are building on an established presence in the area and bringing different areas of expertise from the Rhenus Group under one roof,” said Guglielmo Davide Tassone, Managing Director of Rhenus Overland Italy. The new facility will strengthen Rhenus’ operations in north-eastern Italy and support the coordination of warehouse activities with national and international transport services. The company expects the integrated hub to improve the management of freight flows while providing additional space for future operations.

articles.title: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026
articles.summary: All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers…
articles.body: All American Marine Build Report: October 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Ron Wille, President, All American Marine October 16, 2026 Credit: AAM All American Marine recently launched M/V North Star, the second high-speed, long-range eco-tour vessel built for Phillips Cruises & Tours. Like her sistership, Chugach Express, North Star will operate from Whittier, Alaska, carrying passengers through the tidewater glaciers and wildlife-filled waters of Prince William Sound. The 84.5-foot, hydrofoil-assisted aluminum catamaran features a Teknicraft Design semi-displacement hull and is certified to USCG Subchapter T standards for up to 150 passengers. Her propulsion package mirrors that of Chugach Express: four MJP 350X waterjets driven by quad 800 mhp Scania DI16 082M engines, paired with Teknicraft’s dynamic hydrofoil system and wave-piercing bow. A repeat order is performance data in its clearest form. After operating Chugach Express through three demanding Alaska seasons, with full passenger loads, long days, and changing conditions. Phillips knew this platform could deliver. One of the most notable changes is fuel capacity with Chugach Express carrying 1,200 gallons, while North Star carries 1,600. The increase did not require a redesign; it was made possible by proven performance. Chugach Express demonstrated that the hull could carry additional weight without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or ride quality. The second vessel uses that margin to add 400 gallons and extend its operating range. But range is only part of the story. The Teknicraft hull and dynamic hydrofoil system are designed to reduce vessel accelerations underway, while the hull form and foil provide added motion damping at rest. For passengers, that means a more comfortable ride. For operators, it means a broader usable weather window, supporting more operating days, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. That capability matters in Prince William Sound. Maintaining comfortable speeds in changing sea conditions can preserve more time at the destination while keeping the return schedule within reach. It can also mean the difference between completing a tour and remaining at the dock. Last month, we examined how little fuel consumption changes between light and fully loaded conditions on a Teknicraft hull. North Star shows what an operator can do with that margin. Greater fuel capacity, strong seakeeping, and efficient performance combine to create something more valuable than any single specification: greater operating capacity. WHAT OPERATORS ARE ASKING Top speed tells only part of the story. Passenger vessel operators need to know how a vessel rides at full load in real conditions, how guests feel after five or six hours aboard, and how much of the schedule can be maintained when the weather turns. Those are seakeeping questions, and on a tour vessel, they show up in two places. The first is underway. During transit, the Teknicraft hull form and hydrofoil lift work together to reduce vertical accelerations, the pounding and slamming that wear on passengers and crew over a long day. The second is on scene. At a glacier’s face or alongside a pod of humpbacks, low-speed motion is often when passengers begin to feel unwell. Here, the hull form and foil help dampen that motion. Guests stay on deck, crews remain ready to work, and fewer people become what one of our operators calls “mal de mer zombies.” One additional advantage comes in the adjustable hydrofoil. By de-tuning it, captains can make the vessel ride “heavier” at wildlife-viewing speeds, settling the hull and creating a steadier viewing platform. The vessel remains light and fuel-efficient during transit, then becomes more planted once on scene. Weather is where seakeeping becomes operating capacity. These hulls can maintain comfortable speeds in conditions that force other vessels to slow down or remain at the dock. That broader operating window supports more completed trips, greater schedule reliability, and stronger revenue potential. WHAT IT SIGNALS As Alaska’s tour season winds down, passenger vessel operators head into the off-season with a full season of results in hand. That is when a vessel should be evaluated, by what it delivered through months of real service. What these operators have learned is straightforward: comfort is operating capacity. A vessel that can sail comfortably in more conditions completes more departures, issues fewer refunds, and protects revenue. A vessel that remains steady at low speed keeps guests on deck and engaged. A hull with additional carrying capacity gives operators options, and Phillips Cruises and Tours chose to turn that margin into greater range. Real performance is measured across the entire operating day: at full load, through a full season, and in the weather operators encounter, not the weather they started the season wishing for.

articles.title: Incat Crowther to Build Fourth Fast Support Intervention Vessel
articles.summary: Offshore energy services provider Zamil Offshore has commissioned global digital shipbuilder IncatCrowther and Singaporean shipbuilder Lita Ocean to design, build and deliver a fourth 60-meter ABS-Classed monohull Fast Support Intervention Vessel (FSIV).
articles.body: Incat Crowther to Build Fourth Fast Support Intervention Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Incat Crowther Offshore energy services provider Zamil Offshore has commissioned global digital shipbuilder Incat Crowther and Singaporean shipbuilder Lita Ocean to design, build and deliver a fourth 60-meter ABS- Classed monohull Fast Support Intervention Vessel (FSIV). The project follows the delivery of the third vessel in the original fleet with the performance of the fleet leading to the order of a fourth vessel. The FSIV fleet is assisting Zamil Offshore with the efficient and safe transport of cargo, heavy maintenance equipment and personnel for Saudi Aramco’s operations in the Arabian Sea. Capable of speeds up to 36 knots, the vessels are powered by four MTU 16V4000 diesel engines coupled to ZF gearboxes driving Hamilton HT810 waterjets. Maneuverability of the DP2-certified vessels is enhanced by three Hydromaster tunnel bow thrusters, allowing safe docking and offshore station-keeping for transfer of cargo and personnel. Two of the main engines are coupled to FFS firefighting pumps paired with 1200 m3/hr water monitors and shipboard water spray protection offering FiFi-1 capability. Three Scania 300kW diesel generators provide ship service power. The main deck offers an expansive 250m2 aft cargo deck rated at 2.5 t/ m2 along with an optional Palfinger PK12000M deck crane. A climate-controlled forward cabin features business-class seating for 56 service personnel, as well as two bathrooms, a 15m2 workshop, a 15m2 storage room, a lounge and snack bar. The crew of 20 on the vessel are housed on the hull deck which features a large pantry, mess, three bathrooms and two laundry rooms. The vessels comply with the latest MCVSR requirements from Saudi Aramco, including ABS SMART notation. Construction is now underway on the fourth vessel, with the vessel set to join its predecessors in service by 2027.

articles.title: Carrier stocks push DynaLiners index to 2026 high
articles.summary: The DynaLiners Shares Index rebounded during the latest trading week, gaining 75 points, or 2.8%, to move above the 2,800-point threshold and reach its highest level of 2026. The recovery came despite continued pressure on global trade and economic activity, with container shipping companies providing the strongest...
articles.body: The DynaLiners Shares Index rebounded during the latest trading week, gaining 75 points, or 2.8%, to move above the 2,800-point threshold and reach its highest level of 2026. The recovery came despite continued pressure on global trade and economic activity, with container shipping companies providing the strongest support to the overall index. The DLSI Carriers index climbed 199 points, or 5.1%, to close at 4,081. The result represented another 2026 high and returned the carrier segment to its position as the leading sector index. The remaining sector indices recorded only marginal movements, ranging from a 0.3% decline for DLSI Ports to gains of up to 0.5%. Across the companies tracked by DynaLiners, 67 recorded share-price increases, compared with 51 declines. The average weekly gain stood at 1.9%, although this figure was heavily influenced by Mercantile Ports & Logistics, whose share price surged by 169%. DynaLiners noted that the company’s volatility reflects its low absolute share price, equivalent to approximately US$0.05 even after the increase. Excluding this movement, the average weekly change would have been 0.5%. Carrier stocks dominated the strongest performers. Of the next 15 largest weekly gainers, 13 were container shipping companies, led by Orient Overseas International Limited with a 16% increase. At the opposite end of the ranking, shipowner Seacon declined by 14%, while Vietnam Maritime Corporation recorded the largest loss, falling by 19%.

articles.title: Singapore Conducts Oil Spill Response Drill
articles.summary: Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia conducted a ground deployment exercise (GDX) under the Revolving Fund Committee to strengthen coordination in responding to oil spills in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026…
articles.body: Singapore Conducts Oil Spill Response Drill Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 Credit: Adobe Stock/Peter Hermes Furian Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia conducted a ground deployment exercise (GDX) under the Revolving Fund Committee to strengthen coordination in responding to oil spills in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Conducted ahead of Singapore’s 17th Joint Oil Spill Exercise (JOSE) 2026, the GDX simulated an oil spill originating from a vessel collision in Singapore waters, with the oil subsequently reaching the shores of Indonesia and Malaysia. Led by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the GDX tested information sharing, response planning and mutual assistance among the three littoral States. As part of the exercise, Indonesia and Malaysia deployed response assets in their respective waters to test their response arrangements under the exercise scenario. Separately, MPA hosted representatives from government agencies, industry partners and international organisations at the Integrated Operations Hub (IOH) Lab at ALICE@Mediapolis as part of JOSE 2026. The program provided an opportunity to share Singapore’s oil spill response capabilities and explore how emerging technologies could support future response operations. Representatives from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), ITOPF[1], Indonesia’s Directorate General of Sea Transportation and Malaysia’s Department of Environment also attended the program. Participants were briefed on the coordinated deployment of response assets for oil containment, dispersal and recovery, drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea. The program also highlighted how emerging technologies could enhance oil spill response. These included MPA’s Maritime Digital Twin (MDT), which uses modelling to predict the movement of spilled oil and identify potentially affected areas, as well as artificial intelligence to support response planning and resource deployment. Participants were also briefed on potential concepts of operations involving unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned surface vessels (USVs), including those trialled with ST Engineering. Drawing on demonstrations conducted at sea, the briefing illustrated how aerial surveillance could guide USVs in carrying out tasks such as dispersant spraying and oil containment boom towing. Overall, JOSE explored how such concepts of operations could be supported as unmanned technologies mature, potentially expanding the range of capabilities available for future oil spill response operations.

articles.title: Estonia's First Electric Ferry Takes Shape in Poland
articles.summary: Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard.The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet…
articles.body: Estonia's First Electric Ferry Takes Shape in Poland Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet, will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. Image courtesy Steerprop Steerprop was selected to supply its next-generation contra-rotating propeller (CRP) technology for Estonia's first fully electric passenger ferry, currently under construction at Poland's CRIST SA shipyard. The 95-meter ferry, designed by LMG Marin for the Estonian State Fleet , will feature two Steerprop SP 25 CRP units equipped with permanent magnet motors. The propulsion system is designed to deliver high thrust and improved efficiency in both open water and ice conditions. Steerprop's CRP configuration uses two contra-rotating propellers on a single shaftline, allowing greater thrust and efficiency than comparable single-propeller arrangements. The latest generation introduces pressure lubrication, replacing immersion lubrication to reduce mechanical losses and improve mechanical efficiency by approximately 3.5 percentage points. "The latest Steerprop CRP development has resulted in a propulsor with unique efficiency and thrust performance, and one that offers an even greater performance boost for vessels operating in ice conditions," said Markku Miinala, Steerprop's Cruise & Ferry Segment Director. The ferry will incorporate a 3 MWh battery system charged using renewable shore power, supplemented by biodiesel generators for severe weather and emergency operations. Designed to 1B Ice Class requirements, the vessel will be capable of operating in ice up to 60 centimeters thick. Steerprop already supplies propulsion systems for four double-ended ferries operating on Estonia's Saaremaa and Hiiumaa routes. The propulsion equipment is scheduled for delivery in late 2027, with the ferry expected to enter service in late 2028. The vessel's design and construction contract is valued at €49.93 million, including €28 million in funding from the European Union Modernization Fund, with additional financing from Estonia's CO₂ quota trading mechanisms. articles.title: Anglo-Eastern: World-First Ammonia-Powered Bulk Carrier Enters Service
articles.summary: Anglo-Eastern has detailed its role in developing and preparing CMB.TECH's Mineral Europa, the world's first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, which recently embarked on its maiden voyage.The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding…
articles.body: Anglo-Eastern: World-First Ammonia-Powered Bulk Carrier Enters Service Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding, features a WinGD dual-fuel ammonia engine and a Sun Rui Ammonia Fuel Supply System. Image courtesy Anglo Eastern Anglo-Eastern has detailed its role in developing and preparing CMB.TECH's Mineral Europa, the world's first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier, which recently embarked on its maiden voyage. The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, built by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding, features a WinGD dual-fuel ammonia engine and a Sun Rui Ammonia Fuel Supply System. The vessel can operate on ammonia or conventional marine fuel, providing flexibility as ammonia bunkering infrastructure develops. Anglo-Eastern's involvement dates to 2018, when its technical services division began evaluating alternative fuels with CMB.TECH, initially examining hydrogen before progressing to ammonia. By 2020, Anglo-Eastern Technical Services (AETS) was developing the vessel's safety philosophy, fuel arrangements and preliminary engineering. The design received Approvals in Principle from Lloyd's Register and ABS in 2021. A central engineering challenge was integrating ammonia storage, double-wall piping, ventilation, leak detection, containment and emergency shutdown systems without sacrificing cargo capacity. "The technical challenge was not just accommodating a new fuel. Safety, containment and operational requirements all had to work together as an integrated system without compromising the vessel's primary purpose as a commercial cargo carrier," said Arunava Sengupta, Managing Director of AETS. Anglo-Eastern also supported newbuilding supervision, technical management and crew preparation. Vessel-specific operating, bunkering, maintenance and emergency procedures were developed alongside training incorporating a three-dimensional digital twin, fuel supply simulator and emergency scenarios. Senior officers participated in shipyard and sea trials. "Mineral Europa demonstrates what can be achieved when an owner's conviction is matched by deep engineering and operational capability," said Bjorn Hojgaard, Anglo-Eastern CEO. CMB.TECH CEO Alexander Saverys described the vessel's entry into service as a milestone in the company's decarbonization strategy, with additional ammonia-powered vessels expected to follow. Anglo-Eastern said it remains fuel-agnostic, supporting shipowners in evaluating alternative propulsion technologies according to their operational requirements. Image courtesy Anglo Eastern

articles.summary: Dutch inland shipping company AMS Barging has christened its new diesel-electric tanker Felicitas at Noordereiland in Rotterdam. Liv and Julie, daughters of AMS Barging co-owner Igor Jansen, performed the naming ceremony.The 135-metre tanker…
articles.body: 9,000 m³ Methanol-ready Tanker Christened Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 The 135-m tanker Felicitas was designed by RensenDriessen Shipbuilding and fitted out by Den Breejen Shipyard. Image courtesy AMS Barging Image courtesy AMS Barging Dutch inland shipping company AMS Barging has christened its new diesel-electric tanker Felicitas at Noordereiland in Rotterdam. Liv and Julie, daughters of AMS Barging co-owner Igor Jansen, performed the naming ceremony. The 135-metre tanker was designed by RensenDriessen Shipbuilding and fitted out by Den Breejen Shipyard. With a cargo capacity of approximately 9,000 m³, Felicitas features 12 cargo tanks, a dual piping system, two mass flow meters, a nitrogen generator, a bunker boom and a cargo pumping capacity of 1,800 m³ per hour. The vessel is designed to accommodate future modifications for methanol bunkering. The addition brings AMS Barging’s fleet to 17 vessels. Earlier this year, the inland shipping specialist christened Fortuna, a sister vessel to Felicitas. Geopolitical developments and the energy transition are reshaping the international bunker market. AMS Barging is responding with vessels that can transport conventional fuels while allowing for future changes in fuel demand. “No one knows exactly what the fuel mix will look like in ten years' time. We see methanol as one of the important alternatives,” says Martin van Veen, Commercial Director at AMS Barging. “That is why we invest in vessels that can operate efficiently today while allowing us to respond to future developments.” Felicitas has completed her maiden commercial voyage and is now operating on the spot market. AMS Barging reports strong demand for large tankers capable of transporting substantial cargo volumes efficiently. By carrying larger parcels in a single voyage, Felicitas can reduce the number of vessel movements required and make more efficient use of loading and unloading facilities. The vessel has diesel-electric propulsion and Z-drives, azimuthing propulsion units that improve manoeuvrability. Its engines meet the Stage V emissions standard. AMS Barging has previously reported fuel savings of around 25% with similar diesel-electric propulsion systems, compared with conventionally powered vessels. “With existing vessels, it can sometimes be difficult to find exactly the combination of technology and capabilities we are looking for. By developing newbuild vessels ourselves, we can incorporate the latest technologies and tailor each vessel to the needs of the market. In doing so, we are investing not only in additional capacity, but also in the future of our fleet,” Van Veen said. The AMS Barging team. Image courtesy AMS Barging

articles.summary: Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.

Photo shared by US Central Command By Feras Dalatey and Jonathan Saul DAMASCUS/LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) – Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said. Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters. The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports , the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran’s crude exports. Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July. Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show. The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar’s military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups. Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed. “What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces,” said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI. Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border. The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said. Shelley said the shipments were driven “more by opportunism” than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships. Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia’s Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI’s analysis. The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar’s military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel. US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE ‘IRONCLAD’ The US military’s Centcom said its naval blockade , which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is “ironclad.” The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement. A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added. The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons. Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces. The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said. Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran’s remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products. A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading. Such data “should be taken with a grain of salt,” the spokesperson said. The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was “suffocating the Iranian regime.” Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks. “If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran’s aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries,” Soltvedt added. Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers. REUTERS/Drone Base By Serene Cheong and Nicholas Lua Oct 16, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Accelerating crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz aren’t translating into higher production of a dirty shipping fuel, according to a top Vitol Group executive, tightening supplies and sending prices soaring. The Middle East conflict has reduced fuel oil supply from the Persian Gulf, including from Iran, by 800,000 tons per month, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have cut supply by 1 million tons per month, Vitol’s Asia head Kieran Gallagher said at a conference in Singapore this week. “Many are looking to increased crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz as a silver bullet, but more crude does not necessarily mean more high-sulfur fuel oil,” Gallagher said at Sibcon . “Refining margins are exceptionally strong and refiners have been maximizing throughput to capture those returns,” he added, referring to refiners prioritizing other products such as diesel. The supply squeeze stemming from the two wars has driven prices of high-sulfur bunker fuel made with HSFO in Singapore to the highest level since April, according to data provider ClearLynx LLC. The city-state is the world’s biggest supplier of ship fuel. On Thursday, HSFO costs in Asia soared relative to crude, rising to a seven-month high, according to Bloomberg Fair Value data. Demand for HSFO as a refinery feedstock is adding to the squeeze. North Asian refiners are set to use more than 1 million tons of HSFO to feed upgrading units in November after disruptions to Saudi crude exports from the Red Sea, said Gallagher. Restoring medium and heavy oil supplies to those processors would reduce their reliance on fuel oil as a feedstock and release those barrels back into the bunker pool, he added. Read More: Ship Fuel Market Fragments as Middle East Conflict Hits Trade The picture is less strained for another shipping fuel, low-sulfur fuel oil. That market is “more benign” because China continues to export barrels, while Nigeria’s Dangote refinery has increased its operating rates since August and is exporting two to three Suezmax cargoes per month, Gallagher said. Even there, some pressure remains. Bunker suppliers and traders present at Sibcon said there’s fierce competition for blending components used to reduce impurities, flammability and viscosity in ship fuel to produce LSFO grades. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. According to a regulatory filing dated 15 October 2026, the investment was approved by the company’s Board of Directors and includes eight newbuildings and four resale newbuildings, representing a combined capacity of approximately 114,100 TEU. The smaller ships are classified as resale newbuildings, meaning vessels acquired through resale arrangements rather than conventional secondhand purchases of ships already in service. According to the disclosure, the investment represents approximately 8.16% of HMM’s equity, with the final vessel delivery expected by December 2029. HMM stated that the investment is intended to reinforce its container shipping operations and enhance the competitiveness of its fleet. The announced investment amount and delivery schedule may be subject to adjustments depending on final vessel specifications and delivery arrangements. The regulatory filing confirms approval of the investment programme. However, the Board’s decision should not be interpreted as confirmation that all individual shipbuilding and vessel acquisition contracts have already been executed.

articles.title: Uncertain IMO Rules Weigh on Shipping’s Demand for Cleaner Marine Fuels
articles.summary: Shippers' appetite for lower-carbon marine fuels weakened this year as the fate of a regulatory emissions framework from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) remained cloudy while some are using carbon credits, industry executives said.IMO…
articles.body: Uncertain IMO Rules Weigh on Shipping’s Demand for Cleaner Marine Fuels Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 16, 2026 © Pawinee / Adobe Stock Shippers' appetite for lower-carbon marine fuels weakened this year as the fate of a regulatory emissions framework from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) remained cloudy while some are using carbon credits, industry executives said. IMO member nations are set to meet by early November on the formal adoption of a net-zero framework to guide the industry towards zero carbon emissions by 2050, after last year's vote to delay the move. Demand for marine biofuel, a more readily available alternative fuel on which shippers have focused more, has softened this year at the world's largest bunker hub of Singapore. Marine biofuel sales at the port totalled about 603,000 tons between January and September, down 47% from the corresponding 2025 period, government data showed. Total 2025 volumes had more than doubled from 2024. "I don't expect the biofuel demand to increase so much until we have an IMO decision," said Jens Maul Jorgensen, a director of dry bulk shipowner Oldendorff Carriers. "If anybody wants to have just a slightly greener world, IMO will have to step up," he told Reuters. "What we see now at the moment is a surplus of (carbon) credit to the FuelEU Maritime, and that is competing with biofuel (uptake)," added Jorgensen, speaking on the sidelines of the Singapore International Bunkering conference (SIBCON). He was referring to an EU regulation that requires ships exceeding gross tonnage of 5,000 tons and calling at EU ports to reduce emissions. While the FuelEU Maritime regulation has supported biofuels uptake in the European bunker hub of Rotterdam, the demand increase fell short of expectations. "Some of the tax benefits in Europe have prompted a little more uptake on biofuels, but in general we are a little bit surprised about the lack of demand," said Peter Grunwaldt, chief executive at Cargill-Hafnia joint venture Seascale Energy. "Even though biofuels (post-Iran war) are cheaper than gasoil (on some occasions), we are seeing people stick with gasoil. That's a little bit of a surprise to us, that the demand is not greater," said Grunwaldt. Total bio-blended bunker sales at Rotterdam have risen 28% in the year's first half over the first half of 2025, port data showed. "We need clear regulatory signals for the industry to work with," said Jesper Sorensen, global head of alternative fuels at KPI OceanConnect. "Right now, the only regulatory things in place are the emissions trading system and the FuelEU." The US-Israeli war with Iran has prompted more shippers to continue diversifying supplies, however. "Shipowners who have ordered alternative-fuel tonnage and dual-fuel tonnage are building optionality into their fuel mix," added Sorensen. "The disruption in the Middle East has shown that optionality is a good thing." Fossil-based marine fuel prices this week are at least 70% higher than levels before the Iran war began in February. (Reuters - Reporting by Jeslyn Lerh and Florence Tan; Editing by Clarence Fernandez)

Panoro Energy reported on October 15 the conclusion of drilling two open-water wells to appraise the North-West Hibiscus area at the Dussafu Marin Permit offshore Gabon. articles.body: DP World and Thames Freeport have completed a new £13 million training and innovation centre at London Gateway in the United Kingdom. The facility, known as The Hive, is located within London Gateway Logistics Park. It will support skills development in the maritime and logistics sectors, with plans to train around 1,125 people each year. The project was jointly funded by DP World and Thames Freeport. It aims to help businesses find skilled workers as London Gateway continues to expand. New training facilities for port and logistics workers The Hive includes a training centre equipped with crane operation simulators, virtual reality (VR) technology and facilities for working-at-height training. It will offer more than 100 days of industrial and employment training programmes each year. These programmes will help people develop skills for jobs in ports, logistics and related industries. The three-storey building also includes meeting rooms, an events area and a 100-seat auditorium. Other facilities include a gym and outdoor sports areas for employees working at the port and logistics park. “As the London Gateway Logistics Hub continues to grow, we want to ensure the infrastructure around it grows too,” said Alan Holland, Chief Executive Officer of DP World London Gateway Logistics Park. According to DP World, London Gateway supports more than 10,000 jobs through direct employment and its wider economic activities. Supporting the growth of London Gateway Construction of The Hive began in October 2025. The building has achieved BREEAM Outstanding certification and an EPC A+ energy rating. Training providers and other partners are expected to begin operating from the facility in November 2026. SEATS, which was appointed as the project’s skills partner earlier this year, will work with DP World and local employers to develop training programmes. The new centre forms part of wider efforts to support the growth of London Gateway and strengthen the local workforce.

articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Ports and Logistics Regulatory UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 42 3 minutes read UK Government UK Government British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. London accounted for roughly 500,000 of those, with its growth driven largely by the additional capacity at London Gateway. The DP World terminal handled more than 3m teu in 2025, up 52% from 1.9m teu a year earlier. The increase followed the opening of the fourth berth, which boosted capacity by more than a third, and the arrival of Asia-Europe services operated by Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s Gemini Cooperation in February 2025. London Gateway has been challenging Felixstowe’s position as Britain’s busiest boxport, with Maersk’s departure from the Hutchison-operated facility reshaping the country’s container market. DP World is pressing ahead with another £1bn ($1.33bn) expansion, adding two all-electric berths and a second rail terminal. The BPA argues that such investment and network changes have been overlooked in assessments linking Britain’s expanding container business to EU carbon pricing. The dispute follows research by Spain’s Puertos del Estado, which found the UK’s share of northern European deepsea shipping activity, measured in teu-miles, rose from 17.5% in 2023 to 32.1% by July 2025. Subsequent analysis put the figure at around 36% in the first quarter of 2026, broadly mirroring declines in Germany and the Netherlands. The Spanish study also estimated that 76% of observed route changes were attributable to the EU ETS, raising concerns that containerlines were restructuring their networks to reduce carbon costs. But the BPA has questioned both the methodology and the conclusions. It argues that teu-miles, which combine vessel capacity with voyage distance, measure shipping network activity rather than actual containers handled. The metric can also be distorted by longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and changes to the sequence of port calls. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. Continental European ports have not uniformly lost ground either. Rotterdam’s container throughput increased 3.1% to 14.2m teu in 2025, Hamburg recorded 7.3% growth to 8.3m teu, while Antwerp-Bruges posted a 0.7% increase. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure. Under proposals unveiled in July, certain container ports within 150 nautical miles of an EU port could be excluded from the definition of a port of call for emissions accounting purposes. The threshold for transhipment activity at other qualifying non-EU ports within 300 nautical miles would also be lowered from 65% to 50%. The changes could bring more British terminals within the EU’s anti-evasion framework, potentially increasing carbon costs for shipping lines using them. The proposals have yet to be adopted. “It would be extraordinary if the EU responded to that success by introducing new measures to penalise British ports,” said Mark Simmonds, the BPA’s director of policy and external affairs. The association stressed that it supports shipping decarbonisation but warned against treating normal competition between ports as regulatory avoidance. Britain has already brought domestic shipping and emissions in UK ports into its own emissions trading scheme from July this year, while plans to extend carbon pricing to international voyages from 2028 are also under consideration. The BPA has urged the UK government and the European Commission to reassess the evidence before proceeding with measures that could affect port competitiveness and future investment on both sides of the Channel. Subject to completion and transfer, the vessel is expected to join Stena Line’s Dublin–Liverpool service in early December. Delivery of Somerset is expected later in October....
articles.body: Stena Line has reached an agreement to acquire the RoRo vessel Somerset from CLdN as part of a broader restructuring of its freight network. Subject to completion and transfer, the vessel is expected to join Stena Line’s Dublin–Liverpool service in early December. Delivery of Somerset is expected later in October. The vessel will then enter dry dock for refurbishment and repainting before being renamed Stena Freighter. Somerset previously operated within Stena Line’s network as a chartered vessel. Dublin–Liverpool service returns to one vessel Stena Line currently operates the Rotterdam–Harwich route with two chartered vessels: Mistral, owned by Godby Shipping, and Thuleland, owned by Wallenius SOL. The charter agreements are due to expire, and both ships will be returned to their owners at the end of the year. Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia will subsequently be redeployed from the Dublin–Liverpool route to Rotterdam–Harwich. The North Sea connection will continue to operate with two vessels, both owned by Stena Line. Stena Freighter will replace Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia on Dublin–Liverpool. As a result, the Irish Sea freight route will return to a single-vessel operation after being served by two ships for most of 2026. “We are very pleased with the agreement to acquire Somerset. It’s a vessel that fits well within our network and has the flexibility and capacity to operate on several of our routes,” said Magnus Lander, Head of Network & Business Development at Stena Line. “We know Somerset well from her previous service with us and know what she can deliver. With Somerset, we have an excellent option with significant capacity for the Dublin–Liverpool route,” he added. Lander said the acquisition would also allow Stena Line to strengthen its position on the Rotterdam–Harwich route by deploying Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia. Built by Flender Werft in Germany in 1999, Somerset measures 183.4 metres in length and offers 2,504 lane metres of freight capacity.

articles.body: Americas Europe Tankers International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 415 3 minutes read Bruton Bruton New York-listed tanker owner International Seaways has struck a deal to take over Tor Olav Trøim-backed Bruton in a transaction valuing the Oslo-listed VLCC company at around $370m. The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going considerably further than the sale of two newbuildings first linked to the US owner in market reports last week. International Seaways has secured agreements with shareholders representing 50.5% of Bruton, including Trøim’s Drew Holdings and Koch Inc, to exchange their holdings for newly issued shares in the US company. The exchange is set at 0.0519 International Seaways shares for each Bruton share, with the initial transaction expected to settle around October 20. The remaining shares will be acquired through a merger, with Seaways expecting to issue approximately 3.12m new shares, accounting for 96% of the total consideration. Smaller Bruton shareholders will receive cash at $6.3044 per share. The deal brings four 300,000 dwt VLCCs into the Seaways fold, including the LNG dual-fuel Mount Vision , which entered service in July, and sistership Mount Horizon , scheduled for delivery from China’s New Times Shipbuilding next month. The remaining two vessels, Mount Frontier and Mount Summit , are due in August and October 2027. The first two ships already have substantial charter cover. Mount Vision secured a 3+1+1-year arrangement with a trading house, earning $95,000 per day for the initial nine months before switching to an index-linked structure. Mount Horizon has been fixed for 12 to 15 months at $105,700 per day. The two 2027 newbuildings remain unchartered and have been at the centre of the recent sale speculation. Splash detailed the potential deal last week after Bruton acknowledged market rumours and launched a strategic review. At the time, International Seaways was linked to the purchase of at least two newbuildings, with brokers discussing values north of $200m per vessel. Bruton’s own figures put the original yard cost of the two 2027 ships at about $117m apiece, highlighting how sharply modern VLCC asset values have moved. The $370m announced on Friday, however, represents the valuation of Bruton’s equity rather than the gross value of its vessels. The takeover follows a major restructuring of Trøim’s tanker interests. Bruton originally built up a 12-ship VLCC programme before splitting the business in August, retaining its first four New Times ships and transferring another eight newbuildings into separately listed OMC Tankers. The demerger left Bruton with a concentrated fleet of near-term deliveries, substantial charter cover and financing arrangements with Chinese lessors covering 85% to 90% of construction costs. The eight vessels in OMC Tankers are not part of the International Seaways transaction. For International Seaways, the acquisition continues an aggressive fleet renewal programme that has seen the company dispose of older tonnage while selectively investing in younger ships. The US owner had a fleet of around 70 vessels, including newbuildings, before the deal. It sold seven older tankers, including two VLCCs, earlier this year for more than $216m and has also invested in LR1 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding. The company strengthened its crude tanker trading platform in January by taking full ownership of Tankers International, which subsequently expanded into the suezmax market. The latest acquisition comes against an exceptionally strong earnings backdrop. Alongside the takeover announcement, International Seaways unveiled preliminary third-quarter net income of $340m to $350m, including a roughly $50m gain from the sale of a suezmax. It reported liquidity of approximately $965m at the end of September. The transaction also brings together businesses associated with two familiar names in Norwegian shipping. Family trusts established by John Fredriksen, Trøim’s former longtime business partner, hold a 13.54% stake in International Seaways, according to the latest US regulatory filing. The pair went their separate ways in 2014 after nearly two decades working together. Bruton’s board has unanimously recommended the transaction, with a shareholder vote expected around October 30. Completion is targeted for early November, subject to the necessary approvals, after which Bruton intends to delist from Euronext Growth Oslo. articles.title: Lower emissions do not always signal a more efficient container voyage
articles.summary: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and...
articles.body: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and July 2026. The May voyage generated 3,104 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent emissions while carrying 2,783 TEUs. This resulted in emissions of 1.12 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. By comparison, the July voyage produced 2,547 tonnes of CO₂e and transported 2,077 TEUs. Although its total emissions were 557 tonnes lower, its emissions intensity reached 1.23 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. Consequently, the voyage with the higher absolute emissions transported its cargo more efficiently when emissions were measured against the volume carried. Cargo utilisation shapes voyage emissions efficiency VesselBot said that total CO₂e measures the environmental impact of a voyage but does not indicate how efficiently those emissions were used to transport cargo. To assess voyage emissions efficiency, the company uses Well-to-Wake emissions intensity, measured in grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. The metric relates emissions to the amount of cargo transported and the distance over which it was carried. According to the case study, the average Well-to-Wake emissions intensity across container ship voyages during the second quarter of 2026 was 231.7 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. Average emissions amounted to 651.3 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. VesselBot divided the voyages into six emissions-intensity categories. Voyages in the most efficient category, producing up to 49 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, generated an average of 1,511 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. In contrast, voyages in the least efficient category, producing at least 800 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, emitted an average of 545 tonnes. The most efficient voyages recorded average vessel utilisation of 80% and transported 8,946 TEUs. Average utilisation in the least efficient category fell to 31%, with only 340 TEUs carried. The findings indicate that highly utilised vessels can generate more emissions in absolute terms while distributing those emissions across considerably more transport work. Voyage-level modelling supports accurate comparisons VesselBot noted that emissions-intensity calculations depend on the accuracy of the underlying voyage emissions estimates. Fuel consumption is influenced by vessel characteristics, engine performance, sailing speed, time at sea, port stays and operating conditions. As a result, comparisons based only on voyage distance or general industry averages may not accurately represent individual vessel operations. Combining fuel-consumption modelling with shipment-level cargo data allows emissions to be compared with the transport work delivered by each voyage. According to VesselBot, this approach can help shippers evaluate carriers, services and individual sailings on a more comparable basis. It can also distinguish between a voyage that produces fewer emissions because it transports less cargo and one that genuinely uses fuel more efficiently. The study concludes that absolute emissions and operational efficiency should be treated as separate measures when evaluating the environmental performance of container shipping.

articles.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
articles.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the...
articles.body: Africa Dry Cargo West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada Sam Chambers October 16, 2026 0 731 3 minutes read Winning Winning West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. “West Africa looks set to remain the fastest growing long-haul source of dry bulk cargo,” Tradeviews stated. The growth is already evident. The five West African exporters covered by the consultancy shipped 160.1m tonnes in their principal trades during the first eight months of this year, up 25% year on year. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Bauxite exports, meanwhile, are forecast to retreat from a peak of nearly 194m tonnes this year to 153m tonnes by 2030 as Guinea pushes ahead with domestic alumina processing. A capesize round voyage between Guinea and China takes approximately 78 days, compared with just 29 days on the Australia-China route. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. There are, however, already signs that the region’s growth ambitions are running up against freight market realities. In its latest weekly report, BRS Shipbrokers noted that exceptionally high freight rates had priced some higher-cost Guinean bauxite miners out of the export market. Guinea shipped 15.61m tonnes of bauxite in September, down 12% from August, with freight costs at one point accounting for more than half the delivered value of the commodity. The subsequent easing in capesize rates could provide some relief. The C3 benchmark has fallen from $43.43 a tonne in late September to $32.95 on October 12, prompting BRS to suggest Guinean bauxite exports could recover by 5% to 10% month on month during November and December. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September. SSY has similarly warned that Guinean bauxite exports have retreated from early-September highs, observing that “shipping demand is turning more sensitive to margin levels on the mining side”. Tradeviews did also caution that potential Guinean bauxite export restrictions, Simandou project delays, dedicated ore carriers and the displacement of Australian iron ore shipments could reduce the benefits for the wider capesize market with much of the market increasingly looking like a Chinese conveyor belt. SSY noted in a market report from August that VLOCs of more than 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou shipments during the first half of 2026. More significant for independent owners is what is coming down the slipways. SSY data shows Chinese tonnage accounts for nearly 40% of the current VLOC orderbook, raising questions over how much of Simandou’s enormous prospective tonne-mile demand will ultimately filter through to the conventional capesize spot market. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation
articles.summary: ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind...
articles.body: Subsea October 16, 2026 · 8 hours ago ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email ScottishPower Renewables ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, installing two nearly 1.8-kilometer-long ducts beneath the Suffolk coastline and seabed for the project’s export cables. The ducts, each measuring 800 millimeters in diameter, were installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD), a technique that creates an underground passage without excavating beaches or disturbing the coastline directly. ScottishPower Renewables says the operation involved the world’s longest continuous single sections of extruded polyethylene (PE) ducts and represents the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of duct length and diameter. Manufactured by Pipelife in Norway, the ducts were produced as single uninterrupted lengths, eliminating the need for welded joints. They will provide a protected route for the high-voltage export cables carrying electricity from the offshore wind farm to shore. The landfall works form part of the project’s onshore civil engineering program, led by OCU Group with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. ScottishPower Renewables said the operation also marked a manufacturing record for Pipelife, whose ducts measured approximately 1,793 meters each. “The completion of this colossal HDD, which is three times the length of our other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement – quite literally – and a major milestone as we progress construction of our third windfarm in the region,” said Ross Ovens , ScottishPower Renewables’ Managing Director for Offshore. “Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore windfarm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with our principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark – breaking UK and world records in the process.” The milestone comes as East Anglia Two advances towards offshore construction, with the first export cable expected to be installed in summer 2027, and commercial operation targeted for late 2028. The 960 MW offshore wind farm will be built at a site in the southern North Sea, around 33 kilometers off the Suffolk coast at its nearest point, where 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD wind turbines will be installed on monopile foundations. articles.title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
articles.summary: Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a...
articles.body: Greater China Shipyards GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 56 2 minutes read GSI GSI Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. Shanhaiguan, founded in 1894, specialises in bridge steel structures and railway equipment and operates six production bases across China. Under the agreement, it will allocate fabrication resources to ship blocks and take responsibility for production quality, safety and delivery schedules. Neither the contract value nor the volume of work has been disclosed. The agreement comes with GSI’s production schedule already stretching towards the end of the decade. The Guangzhou-based builder disclosed earlier this year that its contracted business was approaching RMB100bn ($14bn), with overseas orders accounting for more than 95% and construction slots extending into 2030. Its most recent intake includes 10 MR tankers ordered by Greek owner Evangelos Pistiolis’ Central Group, four additional MR vessels for Advantage Tankers and more LNG dual-fuel car carriers for MSC-controlled Global Car Carriers. GSI is also expanding its physical footprint. In May, it signed a joint venture agreement with Guangdong Port and Shipping Group to develop the 360,000 sq m Xiaohudao shipbuilding base in Guangzhou. A separate project launched in September will see a new facility built at Longxue North, with GSI lined up to operate the yard once completed in 2029. The latter is designed to produce up to 18 vessels annually. The Shanhaiguan deal is not an isolated move. Several Chinese bridge and structural-steel manufacturers have entered shipbuilding this year, taking on fabrication work previously handled by established yards. In June, China Railway Baoji Bridge Group’s Yangzhou subsidiary began manufacturing hull sections for a 73,000 dwt self-propelled deck carrier. The project involves 110 blocks across the vessel’s cargo section, with the largest weighing about 190 tonnes. Jingjiang Nanyang Shipbuilding is providing construction coordination, with China Classification Society overseeing technical and quality requirements. Another bridge specialist, Jingjiang Heavy Industry, followed in September, starting work on blocks for a 40,400 dwt bulk carrier. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. Other Chinese shipbuilders have opted to expand fabrication capacity closer to home. Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding commissioned an expansion of its curved-block workshop in late 2025, adding nearly 23,000 sq m of production space. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding also proposed a new block fabrication and assembly facility last year to address capacity constraints and reduce its reliance on external subcontractors. The moves form part of a broader capacity buildout across China. Broker BRS Group identified at least seven dormant shipyards being reactivated and a further dozen established facilities expanding production capacity, developments covered by Splash earlier this year. South Korean builders have been taking similar steps to overcome production bottlenecks. In April, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries introduced a split-hull construction method for a 157,000 dwt suezmax, outsourcing the 168 m bow section to HSG Sungdong Shipbuilding before joining it to a stern section built at Ulsan. HJ Shipbuilding & Construction has also shifted work outside its Yeongdo yard, contracting Daesun Shipbuilding in February to manufacture deckhouse blocks for eight 7,900 teu containerships after its own facilities reached capacity. articles.title: Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology
articles.summary: The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and...
articles.body: Contributions Tech Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology Splash October 16, 2026 0 85 3 minutes read Gerd Altmann via Pixabay Gerd Altmann via Pixabay The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and interpret large volumes of information, compare documents, prepare drafts and help people work through complex tasks. The more important question now is whether organisations are ready to deploy them well. Giving employees access to a general-purpose AI tool is easy. Turning that access into better technical work, stronger compliance and additional team capacity is a management challenge. Leaders must decide where AI should be used, what knowledge it can draw on and where professional responsibility remains. Access is not capability As connectivity improves across fleets, many seafarers can access the same general-purpose AI tools as colleagues ashore, whether or not their company has formally deployed them. A report or proposed response may arrive in polished language without showing what evidence supports it, which company procedure applies or how much was generated by AI. Fluent output is not necessarily useful output. Generic AI can make weak reasoning look convincing or produce material that does not fit the vessel’s actual circumstances. The shore team must then reconstruct the context and verify the basis of what it has received. A generic model does not naturally know which version of a company’s safety management system is current, whether a manual applies to the equipment fitted on a particular vessel or who must approve a proposed SMS change. Specialisation comes from the system built around the model: the company’s knowledge, role-specific instructions, specialist tools, established workflows, permissions and review points. The underlying model may be general-purpose. The operational system should not be. Begin with work that matters The weakest deployment brief is simply to “use AI more”. It leaves each employee to decide what the technology is for, which information is appropriate to use and how much confidence to place in the result. A stronger starting point is a recurring piece of work the team already understands: investigating a technical issue, preparing for an inspection, answering an SMS question or assessing how a new requirement affects company procedures. The task should be meaningful enough to matter but bounded enough to manage. Once the team sees AI supporting a familiar workflow, expansion becomes an operational decision rather than an abstract technology initiative. Let AI do the work around the decision AI is well suited to locating relevant material, assembling context, comparing records, identifying potential gaps and preparing a first draft. People remain responsible for interpreting the evidence, challenging its relevance, resolving uncertainty and approving the action. Its purpose is not to diminish professional expertise, but to extend its reach. A useful shorthand is the 10-80-10 rule. It is not a literal allocation of time or effort, but a sequence for organising the work. In the first 10%, the expert defines the problem, supplies the context and sets the standard for a good outcome. AI carries much of the middle 80% by finding information, structuring it, comparing records and preparing the work. In the final 10%, the accountable professional challenges the result, corrects it and decides what happens next. The percentages should change with the risk. A safety-critical decision may require far more human review than a routine summary. Make adoption a team practice Leaders need to set expectations, appoint owners and create simple feedback loops. Teams should be able to share useful cases, flag weak outputs, and show where information or workflow design needs improvement. In shipping, caution is usually rational. A confident but incorrect answer can waste time or introduce risk. Trust grows when users can inspect the underlying evidence, understand the system’s boundaries and see that their professional judgement remains central. The same discipline should shape measurement. Logins and prompts reveal little. Better questions are whether the team reached a reviewed outcome faster, used relevant company history, avoided duplicate work and captured the decision for the next person. Deployment will create the advantage AI models will keep becoming more powerful and widely available. Access will not be scarce, and it will not provide a durable advantage on its own. The difference will come from deployment: choosing the right work, building specialised systems around it and helping teams incorporate those systems into everyday operations. For leaders, this means treating AI neither as a standalone IT purchase nor as an instruction to reduce headcount. It is an opportunity to give capable people better tools and increase what the organisation can accomplish without weakening accountability. The technology exists. The management challenge is to turn it into a working organisational capability. The shipping companies that do this well will not simply have more people using AI. They will have better-equipped teams, stronger company knowledge and more capacity to act. articles.summary: The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport) announced the appointment of Charlie Cunnion as Port Director. articles.body: Charlie Cunnion Named as Massport Port Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 15, 2026 © Massport The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport) announced the appointment of Charlie Cunnion as Port Director. Cunnion brings over 25 years of leadership experience across global transportation, supply chain management, operations, organizational transformation, and strategic planning. Most recently, he served as Vice President of Supply Chain and Customer Service for CMPC Forest Products North America, where he led a business transformation focused on operational excellence, technology innovation, customer service, and culture change. Cunnion began his career at International Forest Products (IFP), where he rose to the position of Vice President of Global Transportation. While at IFP, he was responsible for 4.2m metric tons of annual freight, logistics service contracts across all modes of transportation and digitization of supply chain processes. In 2024, he joined the joint venture between IFP and CMPC SPA that became CMPC Forest Products North America, where he was the Vice President of Supply Chain Management and Customer Service. Cunnion helped design the new business plan and company framework, oversaw the implementation of a new customer-first operation and reduced supply chain costs by 21 percent. Cunnion is a graduate of Nichols College, where he received Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, Double Major in Economics and Finance. He also was an officer in the U.S Army, rising to the rank of Captain and receiving two Bronze Star Medals during deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. He serves on the board of the Foreign Commerce Club of Boston and the Sharon Cooperative & Nature School. He is also involved with industry associations such as the Northeast Association of Rail Shippers, the Coalition of New England Companies for Trade and the International Forest Products Transport Association. The Port of Boston generates $8.2 billion in annual economic impact and supports more than 66,000 jobs. Keeping the Port competitive to generate future economic growth and support job creation is an essential part of the Authority’s mission. As Port Director, Cunnion will lead Massport's Maritime Division. “Charlie is an expert in supply chain management, with decades of experience across all modes of cargo transportation,” said Massport CEO Rich Davey. “His leadership, experience and strategic perspective will be invaluable to the Port of Boston as we work to strengthen operations and continue a tradition of innovation and growth. I am thrilled to have him on my leadership team and look forward to seeing him build on the success of Conley Terminal and Flynn Cruiseport in his new role.” Conley Container Terminal enables more than 2,500 businesses throughout Massachusetts and New England to ship and receive products globally, including furniture and home goods, footwear, clothing, office supplies, wine and spirits, recycled fibers, sporting goods, seafood and more. In 2025, the terminal strengthened its reach with new international routes, welcomed the largest ships in its history, and moved over 1.7 million metric tons of cargo—underscoring its role in powering regional trade and economic growth. Flynn Cruiseport Boston continues to serve more passengers and cruise ships each year. With over 454,000 passengers and 149 ship calls in 2025, Flynn Cruiseport helped boost economic activity and tourism in the Commonwealth, generating $256 million annually in economic impact and creating over 3,000 jobs. Massport has committed over $100 million toward upgrades at Flynn Cruiseport, including expanding the waiting area with increased seating capacity and restrooms, streamlining the security check-in and installing a new escalator to improve passenger flow. As larger ships visit the region, the Cruiseport will be prepared for the future. Massport also announced a plan to bring ship-to-shore power to the Cruiseport by 2030. Nearly 80 percent of the ships that currently serve Boston can plug into shore power or use alternative low-carbon technology. When ships use shore power, they tap landside electricity for their power needs at berth including lights, pumps, communications, and refrigeration, instead of running diesel-fueled auxiliary on-board engines.
